opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think tokenizers are kind of the clearest example of a hand-engineered component that we've just accepted as part of the pipeline, and when you look closely at the failure modes, they all point in the same direction.

Think about the classic issues people run into: models that can't count the letters in a word, that struggle with arithmetic because numbers get chunked in weird, inconsistent ways, that behave differently depending on whether there's a leading space, or that are much less efficient and less capable on languages and domains that were underrepresented when the tokenizer's vocabulary was built. Things like code, DNA, or other non-English text. There are also the "glitch token" phenomena, where some token exists in the vocabulary but barely appears in training, so the model does bizarre things when it sees it.

What all of these have in common is that they're not really failures of the model. They're failures of a fixed, heuristic preprocessing step that sits outside of learning. BPE is a compression algorithm run once on some corpus with a frequency heuristic, and then it's frozen. The model never gets to decide how to segment its input. It just has to live with those decisions, even when they're bad for the task.

So to me that's a pretty strong argument for the broader principle in deep learning, which is that whenever you replace a handcrafted feature with something learned from raw data, things eventually get better as you scale. We saw it in vision, moving from engineered features to learning from pixels, and in speech. Tokenization is one of the last big holdouts of that kind of manual feature engineering in language modeling.

The ideal is a model that operates on something close to the raw signal, like bytes, and learns its own chunking or abstraction dynamically, figuring out which parts of the input deserve more computation and how to group things into meaningful units, in a way that adapts to the data and the task. That's part of why I've been interested in architectures that can handle long raw sequences efficiently, like state space models, and in hierarchical approaches that learn the segmentation end to end. If you can do that, many tokenizer problems should disappear rather than needing patches one by one, and I think you'd also get better scaling and robustness across modalities where there isn't an obvious tokenization at all.

r001.rationale: The response links tokenizers’ chunking of words into units to models’ difficulty counting letters, identifying tokenization as a cause of character-level problems.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to frame this is that tokenization is really the one piece of the modern language model pipeline that is still hand-engineered. Everything else, we've learned to trust that if you give the model enough data and the right architecture, it will figure out the features it needs. But at the very front of the pipeline, we still have this heuristic preprocessing step, usually something like BPE, that chunks bytes into subword units based on frequency statistics. And that's a design decision that someone made, not something the model learned.

And once you look at it that way, a lot of the weird failure modes of language models start to look like symptoms of that decision rather than fundamental limitations. The classic example is the model can't count the letters in "strawberry," or it struggles with spelling, or with simple character-level manipulations. That's because it literally never sees the characters. It sees these opaque IDs, and the relationship between the token and its constituent characters has to be inferred indirectly. You also get a lot of brittleness: tokenizers are tuned for English and for typical web text, so if you go to other languages, or code, or math, or anything that isn't well represented, the segmentation gets worse and the model effectively pays more compute per unit of meaning. And then there are these adversarial or just unlucky cases, like glitch tokens or the fact that adding a trailing space completely changes how a string is tokenized, where the model behaves in ways that have nothing to do with language and everything to do with the artifact we put in front of it.

So to me the argument goes like this. We have a long history in deep learning of hand-crafted features getting replaced by learned ones, and every time that's happened the learned version eventually won, because it adapts to the data instead of to our priors about the data. Tokenization is basically the last feature-engineering step left. The problems it causes are evidence that the prior we baked in is wrong in a bunch of places. And the natural response is to push the learning all the way down to raw bytes and let the model decide how to chunk and compress its input.

The reason that hasn't happened yet is efficiency, not principle. If you operate on bytes, your sequences get something like four or five times longer, and with attention that cost is quadratic. Tokenization is really an efficiency hack to get sequence lengths down to something tractable. So the question that I find exciting is: can you build architectures that do that compression themselves, in a learned way, as part of the model? That's what motivates a lot of our work on state space models and on things like hierarchical or dynamic chunking, where the model learns to form its own boundaries based on content rather than fixed statistics. If you can do that, you get the efficiency benefits of operating over compressed units, but the units are learned end to end, and they can be different for different data and different contexts.

And the hope is that this isn't just about fixing the strawberry problem. It's that if the model controls its own abstraction hierarchy, you might get better scaling, better robustness across languages and modalities, and a more unified story where the same model can ingest text, code, DNA, audio, whatever, without someone having to design a tokenizer for each one. So the tokenizer problems are kind of the smoke, and end-to-end learning from raw data is where I think the fire is.

r001.rationale: The response says tokenization chunks bytes into subword units and that the model sees opaque IDs rather than characters, linking this to difficulty counting letters, spelling, and character-level manipulations.

astra-6.text:
I think tokenization is a good example of how a preprocessing decision can make learning easier in one sense, but also introduce constraints that the model can’t undo. We take a string of text and split it into these discrete units using a fixed procedure, before the model ever sees it. And that procedure doesn’t necessarily line up with the structure you want the model to learn.

For example, two very similar words can be broken into completely different tokens. Or a number might be split in a way that obscures its digits. Then we ask why a model struggles with spelling or certain arithmetic tasks, when the representation we gave it makes that information harder to access.

That’s the motivation for learning from raw data: let the model learn the representation along with the task, rather than hard-coding that boundary. Of course, the tradeoff is efficiency. If you work directly with bytes, your sequences get much longer. So tokenizers serve a very practical purpose today. But I think the interesting research question is whether we can build architectures that process those longer sequences efficiently and learn their own useful abstractions.

r001.rationale: The response says text is split into fixed tokens before the model sees it, and that this can make spelling information harder to access. Its examples of similar words receiving different tokens and numbers losing digit structure communicate how tokenization above the character level can hinder character-level reasoning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think tokenization is a good example of how a preprocessing decision can introduce a lot of complexity into a model. You take the raw text and impose this fixed vocabulary on it before learning even starts. And that choice affects how the model sees different languages, how it handles numbers, how it deals with spelling—whether two things that are very similar at the character level look similar at all to the model.

If you think about some of the strange weaknesses of language models, like counting characters in a word, tokenization makes those tasks unnecessarily awkward. The model doesn’t actually see the characters directly; it sees these chunks that were chosen by a separate procedure.

So the argument for learning from raw data is: could we let the model learn the right representations and the right level of abstraction itself? That doesn’t mean you have to do all the computation at the byte level. Ideally, you would read the raw input, learn how to compress it into useful higher-level representations, and do most of your reasoning there. There are real efficiency challenges, but I think that’s a more natural direction than hard-coding that first step.

r001.rationale: The response says tokenization presents text as chunks rather than individual characters, making tasks like counting characters unnecessarily awkward for language models.
